html:
Sufism is the inward, mystical path within Islam, which seeks closeness to God through prayer, self-discipline and love. Its practices centre on dhikr, the remembrance of God by repeating His names, often with music, chant or movement.

It grew from the ascetics of the 700s, such as Rabia of Basra, who taught love of God for His own sake. Masters in Baghdad in the 800s and 900s worked out its ideas. The theologian al-Ghazali, who died in 1111, wrote it firmly into mainstream Sunni Islam.

From the 1100s Sufis gathered into orders, called tariqas, each tracing a chain of teachers back to the Prophet Muhammad:

  • the Qadiriyya, from Baghdad, one of the most widespread;
  • the Chishti order in India;
  • the Mevlevi order of Konya, founded on Rumi's teaching, known for its turning dervishes;
  • the Naqshbandiyya of Central Asia.

Sufi teachers, traders and shrines carried Islam into India, Central Asia, Africa and Southeast Asia, often blending with local customs. Sufism shaped great poetry: Rumi, Hafez, Amir Khusrau and Bulleh Shah. It also spread coffee, which Sufis in Yemen drank in the 1400s to stay awake for night prayers (see coffee reaches Yemen). Its music lives on in qawwali and in shows like Coke Studio Pakistan. Some reformers have attacked saint shrines as un-Islamic, and Turkey closed the Sufi lodges in 1925.
sum: Sufism is the inward, mystical path within Islam, which seeks closeness to God through prayer, self-discipline and love. Its practices centre on dhikr, the remembrance of God by repeating His names, often with music, chant or movement.
